Sanofi signs the biggest pharma takeover in three years: $41 billion for US-based Insmed, its shares soar 10.9%

French drugmaker Sanofi announced on Tuesday, November 24, that it is buying US-based Insmed, a specialist in respiratory diseases, for about $41 billion in cash, or $175 per share. The goal: prepare for life after Dupixent, its flagship drug, which will lose its patent protection. In Paris, Sanofi shares jumped 10.9% [1][2].
Sanofi is paying $175 per Insmed share, or about $41 billion (€37.6 billion) for the shares. That is 46% above the price on November 18, the day before the first press leaks [1].
It is the biggest pharma takeover since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in 2023, according to CNBC [2], and Sanofi's biggest deal since its merger with Aventis in 2004 [1].

Insmed brings two drugs already on the market, Brinsupri and Arikayce, and a phase 3 candidate, TPIP [1]. Brinsupri, which treats a chronic lung airway disease, brought in about $1.09 billion between its US launch in August 2025 and September 30, 2026 [1].
Sanofi CEO Belén Garijo cites "combined peak sales potential of more than $10 billion" and more than $500 million in savings per year [4].
Sanofi will pay with cash and debt. JPMorgan and BNP Paribas are sharing a $35 billion bridge loan, according to Bloomberg [3].
At the close, Insmed was up 14.1% at $170.15 in New York, and Sanofi up 10.9% in Paris [2], its biggest one-day gain since 2008 according to Boursorama [15].
Both boards have approved the deal. Sanofi says its 2026 financial targets are unchanged [1].

Key takeaway: Sanofi depends on a single drug, Dupixent, for eczema and asthma. Its main US patent expires in March 2031 [9]. Sanofi's chief financial officer admitted it: the lost sales are "too large to be offset" [9]. So the group is buying drugs that are already selling.

The stock market cheered, which is rare for the buyer in a big takeover. Barclays analysts say the deal clearly improves Sanofi's outlook as the Dupixent patent expires [2]. The deal also lifted the whole sector: the New York stock market's healthcare index gained 2.6% [7].

Insmed is not a research bet: Brinsupri brought in $917 million in the first nine months of 2026, and Insmed is targeting $1.35 billion to $1.4 billion for the year [6]. It is the biggest biopharma takeover of the year [8], and another European purchase in the United States, the world's largest drug market.
The takeover still needs approval from Insmed shareholders and regulators, with completion expected in the first half of 2027 [1][2].

Sanofi is the biggest healthcare stock in the CAC 40: if you have a PEA or a life insurance policy invested in French shares, you probably own a little of it. Its 10.9% jump helped the Paris stock market on Tuesday. As a patient, nothing changes for you: these respiratory drugs are mostly sold in the United States.

How it works: why the target trades below the offer price

Sanofi is promising $175 per Insmed share, but the stock ended Tuesday at $170.15 [1][2]. The gap, about 2.8%, pays for the wait and the risk: the money will only be paid at completion, expected in the first half of 2027, and the deal can still fail if shareholders or regulators say no [1][2]. Specialized funds, known as "arbitrage" funds, buy the target to collect this gap. The smaller the gap, the safer the market considers the deal. The 46% premium, meanwhile, is calculated on the November 18 price, before the rumors [1]: in the meantime, Insmed shares had already climbed.
Precedents: when pharma buys its growth
February 16, 2011
Sanofi-Aventis buys US-based Genzyme, a rare-disease specialist, for $74 per share, or about $20.1 billion, plus a bonus of up to $3.8 billion if targets are met [12][13].
Sanofi has bought a growth driver in the United States before: Genzyme became its rare-disease unit.
September 4, 2025
Sanofi shares fall about 10% after disappointing phase 3 results for amlitelimab, one of its hopes to succeed Dupixent [16].
When in-house research disappoints, drugmakers turn to takeovers.
December 14, 2023
Pfizer completes its takeover of cancer specialist Seagen for $229 per share, a value of about $43 billion, after regulators gave conditional approval [10][11].
These mega-deals take months: the Insmed deal will only close in 2027.

Iraq: Baghdad orders the takeover of Kurdish border crossings and oil fields, Erbil says it is "in no way acceptable"

On Tuesday, November 24, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the federal state to take control of all border crossings in Kurdistan and to manage oil fields in four provinces held by Kurdish forces. He is responding to an investigation into oil smuggling. The Kurdish government rejects these orders [1][2][4].

The decision hands the federal Oil Ministry the fields located in the provinces of Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh [1]. These fields are outside the autonomous Kurdistan Region, but remain under its "security authority" [3].
The federal border crossings authority is to take charge of all crossing points in Kurdistan, government spokesman Sabah al-Numan said; border guards are to close unofficial crossings [3][5].
The Kurdish government will no longer be able to authorize exports of crude oil or oil products without the approval of the federal Oil Ministry [1][4].

The head of the border crossings authority was fired, and the director general of the North Oil Company, the state-owned northern oil company, was suspended along with his deputies pending the smuggling investigation [1][3].
The statement does not say when or how the takeover will happen [3].

Masrour Barzani, Prime Minister of Kurdistan, calls these orders "truly surprising and in no way acceptable" [4]. Masoud Barzani, leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), warns that the region "will not submit to unconstitutional decisions" [6].
According to Reuters sources, Kurdish authorities are expected to resist, citing the absence of a national oil and gas law [2].
Key takeaway: Baghdad is going after the core of Kurdish autonomy, oil and customs revenue, at the risk of a new crisis with Erbil [2][4].

This decision extends Ali al-Zaidi's campaign against smuggling: a few days earlier, on November 20, government forces entered a stronghold of the pro-Iranian militia Kataib Hezbollah near Baghdad, accused along with senior officials of an oil smuggling scheme that had lasted for years [2][7].

Kurdish oil is an explosive issue. Exports through the pipeline to the Turkish port of Ceyhan only resumed on September 27, 2025, after a deal between Baghdad, Erbil and foreign companies: about 180,000 to 190,000 barrels per day of Kurdish crude were then to go through Iraq's state oil marketer SOMO [8]. In April 2026, Iraq was targeting 340,000 barrels per day in total through this pipeline [9].
This is not the first showdown: in 2017, after the Kurdish independence referendum, Baghdad took back all the Kirkuk fields, including Bai Hassan and Avana [10].

Kurdish oil goes through Turkey and reaches the Mediterranean, so close to Europe. If the standoff blocks these barrels, that means slightly less supply at a time when Hormuz is already disrupted: enough to make your tank of fuel more sensitive to bad news.

Mayors' congress: presidential candidate David Lisnard seeks re-election as head of the AMF this Wednesday, and his dual role is ruffling feathers

The 108th Congress of French Mayors is being held in Paris from November 24 to 26. Voting for the presidency of the Association of French Mayors (AMF) closes this Wednesday, November 25, at 1 p.m.: outgoing president David Lisnard, who is also running for the Élysée, faces Philippe Laurent, mayor of Sceaux [1][2][3].

Voting is entirely online, from Monday, November 23, at 5 p.m. to Wednesday, November 25, at 1 p.m. It also renews the association's Bureau and Steering Committee [4]. The result is due on Wednesday at 2 p.m. [1].

David Lisnard, mayor of Cannes, is seeking a new term while he is the Nouvelle Énergie party's candidate in the 2027 presidential election [3][5]. He was first elected head of the AMF in 2021, with 62.3% of the vote [6].
He faces a single rival: Philippe Laurent, UDI mayor of Sceaux, in the Hauts-de-Seine [3].

Many elected officials see it as a "mixing of roles" [5]. "He should have kept the two separate," sums up one mayor quoted by Public Sénat [7]. David Lisnard says he will step back from the AMF during the campaign if needed [3].

Most presidential candidates plan to attend the congress, except Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon [2]. It is hard to skip "the largest gathering of local elected officials in Europe" when you are seeking the 500 sponsorships needed to run [1][2].
The 2027 budget is on the congress agenda [4]. Facing criticism from mayors, the government wants to highlight its record on simplifying regulations [1].
Key takeaway: the mayors' congress has become a stop on the race for the Élysée, and the head of their association is himself a candidate [1][5].

Mayors are key players in the presidential election: their signatures, the "sponsorships," are required to run [1]. Their association, the AMF, also carries weight in debates over municipal funding: this year the AMF is launching "a new call for local freedoms" [8].

The regulations issue is an old one. At the November 2025 congress, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised two "mega-decrees" to scrap around a hundred regulations [9][10]. He also warned that having no budget would mean "zero state equalization, no investment grants" for municipalities [11].
This year, the Senate reduced the effort asked of local authorities in the 2027 budget bill [12]. The text still has to go back and forth between the two houses of Parliament.

What happens at the congress affects your municipality: the money the state gives it funds schools, canteens, roads and daycare. If grants fall, your town hall may cut some services or raise property tax. And it is also partly where it is decided who will be able to run for the Élysée.

Nigeria: central bank holds its rate at 23%, fearing the election campaign and the holidays will push prices up again

On Tuesday, November 24, in Abuja, Central Bank of Nigeria Governor Olayemi Cardoso announced that the policy rate would stay at 23%. Inflation has been falling for five months, but the committee fears that spending linked to the elections and the year-end holidays could push it back up [1][3][4].

The Monetary Policy Committee of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) held its 308th meeting on November 23 and 24; it is leaving the policy rate, which guides the cost of credit in the country, at 23% [1][3][5].

All other settings remain the same: the "corridor" around the rate (+0.5 points and -3 points) and the reserve requirements, the money banks must lock up at the central bank: 45% of deposits for commercial banks, 16% for merchant banks and 75% for certain public deposits [1].
Olayemi Cardoso highlights five straight months of falling inflation and better transmission of the bank's decisions to the economy; the priority remains to continue this "disinflation" [3].
The committee warns that election-related spending and holiday spending could push prices back up [4].
The decision was expected: all five experts polled by the Nairametrics website before the meeting were betting on a hold at 23% [5].
In September, at its 307th meeting, the central bank made a bold move, cutting its rate by 3.5 points in one go, from 26.5% to 23% [2][6].
Key takeaway: after a sharp cut in September, Abuja is hitting pause, fearing that campaign and holiday money will push prices up again [2][4].

It has come a long way. A year ago, in November 2025, the central bank was still holding its rate at 27% despite slowing inflation [7]. It then cut it to 26.5% in February 2026, then to 23% in September [8][2].

For Nigerian businesses and households, a 23% rate is still very high: borrowing is expensive, which holds back investment. But the central bank believes inflation is not yet under enough control to go further, especially ahead of a period of heavy spending [3][4].
The central bank is also keeping very heavy reserve requirements, up to 45% of commercial banks' deposits: that is money that cannot be lent, another brake on inflation [1].

For you, the effect is indirect: if you have family in Nigeria, investments in emerging-market funds, or if your company works with the country, a stable rate signals that the central bank wants to protect purchasing power and the currency first before making credit cheaper.

news.2026-11-25-afrique-du-sud-phala-pha: South Africa: judgment day for Ramaphosa, who wants to overturn the report paving the way for his impeachment

The Western Cape High Court is due to rule this Wednesday, November 25, on whether to set aside the 2022 report that paves the way for impeachment proceedings against President Cyril Ramaphosa in the so-called "Phala Phala" affair [1][2].
This expert report found that the president had a case to answer on four possible charges [3].
His lawyers argue that the panel applied the wrong legal test, relied on unverified evidence and exceeded its mandate [3].

In May, the Constitutional Court overturned the 2022 vote by lawmakers that had buried the affair [4]. Since July 24, a court order obtained by Ramaphosa has blocked the impeachment committee, made up of 31 lawmakers from 16 parties [5].
Key takeaway: an unfavorable ruling would revive impeachment proceedings against the head of state [1][5].

The day before, speaking to the National Council of Provinces (the upper house of Parliament), Ramaphosa said 60% of the 30 reform projects in his "Vulindlela" plan were completed or on track, five weeks before his country is excluded from the US trade deal AGOA on January 1, 2027 [6].
If you buy South African wine or fruit, a political crisis that weakens the rand can affect their price on the shelf.

news.2026-11-25-maroc-madagascar-sahara-: Morocco: Madagascar backs the autonomy plan for the Sahara and signs nine agreements in Rabat

Meeting on Monday, November 23, in Rabat for the second joint commission between the two countries, Morocco and Madagascar signed nine agreements and memorandums, and Antananarivo reaffirmed its support for Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara [1][2][3].
The meeting was co-chaired by Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and his Malagasy counterpart, Alice N'Diaye [1].
The texts cover customs cooperation, trade, industry, agriculture, tourism and handicrafts [1][4].
Morocco is raising the number of scholarships offered to young Malagasy students from 90 to 200, starting with the next academic year [1].
Madagascar welcomes UN Security Council Resolution 2797, which cites autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as a possible solution [1][3].
Key takeaway: Rabat keeps winning African countries over to its position on Western Sahara, relying on the latest UN resolution [1][2].
The political support comes with concrete cooperation, from customs to tourism, and an effort on training young Malagasy people [1][4].
Western Sahara poisons relations between Morocco and Algeria, two countries with close ties to France: each new backer weighs on an issue that also affects Paris.
